newsitem.title: GERMANY: Popular Lamfalussy a tough act to follow at EMI.
newsitem.headline: Popular Lamfalussy a tough act to follow at EMI.

text.p: Alexandre Lamfalussy, the diminutive outgoing head of the European Monetary Institute, leaves behind a professional and personal record that will make him a tough act for tall Dutchman Wim Duisenberg to follow.

The 68-year-old Belgian, whose soft-spoken manner belies his reputation as a straight-talking and influential monetary policy expert, received accolades as he ended his three and a half year tenure as the EMI's first president on Monday.

"One of your greatest assets is that you managed to combine this typical conservative and cautious nature of a central banker, alway focused on substance, with your firm belief in European monetary integration," Duisenberg said at a farewell ceremony attended by Europe's top bankers.
Duisenberg, the Dutch central bank governor who has taken a tough line on inflation, officially takes up the reins at the EMI on Tuesday.
In less than 12 months the institute is likely to be superseded by the European Central Bank ahead of the planned euro launch in January 1999.

He inherits an institute which is broadly regarded as having done a solid job in the tough task of preparing the ground for economic and monetary union (EMU) since it began operations on January 1, 1994.

Under Lamfalussy, the EMI has produced a well-received blueprint for the ECB and issued copious reports on technical issues. But it has also supplied a pragmatic voice on the challenges of currency union -- often a welcome relief from gung-ho political rhetoric.

"In politics or economic life there is no such thing as 100 percent certainty," was Lamfalussy's response earlier this year to the increasingly fraught issue of whether the EMU timetable can be kept to in times of unemployment crises.
The EMI head also issued a stern rebuke to governments for failing to get their budgets in order to meet the tough convergence criteria viewed as essential to secure a strong common currency.
His comments were typical for the man once labelled in the British press as the "central bankers' central banker".
Addressing Monday's ceremony, Lamfalussy steered clear of controversy, confining himself to highlighting the "ethically unacceptable" unemployment levels in most European countries.
"Reducing unemployment must be the prime objective of action by authorities," Lamfalussy said, while cautioning that monetary policy had little power to create jobs.

A professor at Belgium's University of Louvain, a former visiting lecturer at Yale and an Oxford graduate, Lamfalussy's academic credentials are as impressive as his record in steering Europe's monetary and banking strategy.

His firm support for fixed exchange rates and the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) earned the Hungarian-born banker the full endorsement of Europe's central bankers to be the first head of the EMI as it started operations in January 1994.

Lamfalussy was then general manger of the Basle-based Bank for International Settlements, where he was credited with steering a traditionally conservative institution into a more active role in regulatory issues, and had spent years as a commercial banker in Belgium.
Once the Frankfurt ceremonies are over, Lamfalussy plans to return to his academic roots.
The banker, who always planned to retire before the planned EMU launch on January 1, 1999, is going back to the University of Louvain where he plans to spend time writing books.
